readingInstruction: Read 2 Samuel 13:1-14:33. These chapters show the first consequences of David’s sin: violence and division within his own house. Read them with sorrow. They are painful.
settingTheScene: Nathan told David that “the sword shall never depart from your house” (12:10). Chapters 13 and 14 show that word beginning to come true. David’s son Amnon rapes his half-sister Tamar. Her brother Absalom murders Amnon, and flees. After three years, Joab arranges for Absalom’s return. The family that David has built is breaking apart.
observation: Amnon desires Tamar, and on the advice of Jonadab, pretends to be ill and asks that Tamar bring him food (13:1-9).
Tamar says, “No, my brother, do not violate me, for such a thing is not done in Israel” (13:12).
Amnon rapes her and then hates her “with very great hatred” and throws her out (13:14-17).
“When King David heard of all these things, he was very angry” (13:21). He does nothing.
Absalom says nothing to Amnon, “either good or bad,” for he hated him (13:22).
After two years, Absalom has Amnon killed at a sheep-shearing feast, and flees to Geshur (13:23-38).
A wise woman of Tekoa, sent by Joab, tells David a story about two sons, so that he will bring Absalom back (14:1-20).
Absalom returns, but David will not see him for two years, and when they finally meet, “the king kissed Absalom” (14:28-33).
interpretation:
These chapters are among the saddest in the Bible. The violence in David’s house echoes his own sin. A son takes what he wants from a woman. A father fails to act. Another son murders in revenge. The pattern of David’s sins, desire, deception, and bloodshed, is repeated by his children. Children often imitate what their parents have done, and they usually take it further.

Tamar is the innocent victim. Her words to Amnon are wise and clear, and she even tells him to ask the king to give her to him in marriage. He will not hear. After the assault, she tears her robe and puts ashes on her head and lives “a desolate woman” in Absalom’s house. The Bible does not minimize her pain. Her story reminds readers that the effects of abuse are real, and that God sees. Her cry, “Where could I carry my shame?” is heard.

David’s failure is the lack of action. “He was very angry,” says the text, but he does nothing. The Greek and Dead Sea texts add that he did not rebuke Amnon “because he was his firstborn and he loved him.” David’s own guilt may have left him unable to discipline his sons. A leader who has lost moral authority through unrepented sin cannot easily correct others.

Absalom’s two years of silence is a picture of bitterness that is growing. Then the murder. His flight and the ensuing exile set the stage for the rebellion in chapters 15 to 18. David’s half-hearted attempt to deal with the matter, bringing Absalom home but keeping him from his presence, solves nothing. Reconciliation without truth does not heal.

The tragedy is that David’s confession and God’s forgiveness did not remove the consequences. Forgiveness restores our relationship with God. It does not undo what we have set in motion. This is why sin is so serious, and why the cross is so necessary.
connection: Jesus is the opposite of David as a father and king. He defends the vulnerable and rebukes oppressors (Matthew 23:14; Mark 9:42). He is the one who “binds up the brokenhearted” (Isaiah 61:1; Luke 4:18). Hebrews 12:15 warns against a “root of bitterness” that causes trouble. Ephesians 4:26-27 warns against letting anger give the devil a foothold. Galatians 6:7 says, “Whatever one sows, that will he also reap.”
application:
If you are a parent or leader, ask where you have failed to act when you should have.

Pray for those who have suffered abuse. Ask God to help you listen and believe.

Examine any bitterness you are nursing, and bring it to God before it grows.
prayerPrompts: Pray for those who have been wronged, and for comfort for the desolate.
Ask him to keep you from nursing bitterness.
Ask him to give leaders courage to act justly.
